title: Subquadratic factor-three edit-distance approximation
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Does there exist a classical randomized algorithm and constants \(\eta>0\) and \(C>0\) such that, for every pair of explicitly given strings \(X,Y\) of total length \(n\), the algorithm runs in at most \(C(n+2)^{2-\eta}\) time and, with probability at least \(2/3\), outputs an estimate \(\widehat d\) satisfying \[\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\leq\widehat d\leq3\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)?\]

source_formulation.text: Recent developments in designing fast approximation algorithms \([2, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 25]\) culminated in an \(O(1)\)-approximation in near-linear time [3], but the existence […]

context:
Andoni and Nosatzki obtain \(O(n^{1+\gamma})\) time for every fixed \(\gamma>0\), with an approximation constant depending on \(\gamma\). Their theorem does not bound that constant by three. This is the known result preceding the source’s truncated question.

Goldenberg, Rubinstein and Saha obtain a \(3+o(1)\) approximation in \(n^{1.6+o(1)}\) time without preprocessing. Despite the paper’s title, this is a result in the ordinary input model. Its approximation factor approaches three from above and therefore does not certify the exact factor-three guarantee.

Mao and Rubinstein give a randomized \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), in time \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{\Omega(1)}}\), with high probability. The demonstrated saving is subpolynomial in \(n\). Their theorem crosses the factor-three accuracy threshold but does not establish \(O(n^{2-\eta})\) time for any fixed \(\eta>0\).

The original paper also studies edit distance with cheaper substitutions and bicriteria guarantees involving substitution and insertion/deletion budgets. Those positive results concern a different cost model or additional parameters. The selected introductory question uses ordinary unit-cost distance on unrestricted inputs.
why: Tests how much accuracy can be retained while obtaining a fixed polynomial speedup for a basic sequence-comparison problem. It separates the power of approximation from the quadratic barrier for exact computation, with relevance to algorithms for aligning and comparing strings.
status_note: Read the complete original introductory question and its full author counterpart, the Andoni–Nosatzki full-version main theorem, the Goldenberg–Rubinstein–Saha ordinary-input result, and the full March 2026 paper’s tradeoff table and Theorem 6.1. Verified the STOC 2026 publisher date. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no fixed-power-time factor-three resolution. The sequential model and constant success probability make explicit the randomized algorithmic target; no near-linear-time requirement is imposed.

progress.text: Near-linear time becomes possible with an arbitrary parameter-dependent constant factor, while another result reaches factor 3+o(1) in truly subquadratic time.
The source explicitly retains a truly subquadratic factor-three approximation as open.
The STOC approximation-scheme result achieves factors arbitrarily close to one, with a subpolynomial saving from quadratic time.

sentences: The task compares two arbitrary explicit strings using unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions.
The estimate must lie between the true edit distance and three times that distance.
The algorithm must save a fixed positive power over quadratic time on every input.
Known truly subquadratic algorithms approach factor three from above.
The 2026 approximation scheme achieves better accuracy, but its proved time saving is smaller than a fixed power of the input length.

definitions:
The unit-cost Levenshtein edit distance \(\operatorname{ED}(X,Y)\) is the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to transform \(X\) into \(Y\). Each operation costs one, including substitution. There are no transpositions, moves of blocks, or cheaper substitution costs. The two strings can have different lengths or be empty.

The input consists of both strings in full, with their lengths. Let \(n=|X|+|Y|\). Characters can be encoded by integer labels in \(\{1,\ldots,\max\{1,n\}\}\); only equality of labels matters. This allows arbitrary alphabets occurring in the input, rather than a binary-alphabet promise. Renaming polynomially bounded integer symbols takes only a near-linear preprocessing cost, which is included.

Use the usual sequential random-access model with \(O(\log(n+2))\)-bit words: a word read or write, comparison, Boolean operation, shift, or arithmetic operation on a constant number of words costs one step. Memory is initially empty except for the input; reading the input, all preprocessing and writing the output are charged. The algorithm has independent fair random bits, but no advice or uncharged preprocessed strings, distance oracle, parallel processors or quantum operations.

One uniform algorithm and fixed constants must work at every input length, for every input pair and every distance regime. Its running-time bound holds for every random tape. The probability of meeting the approximation guarantee is over its internal randomness alone; the inputs need not be random or generated by a mutation model.

The estimate may be an integer: rounding a valid nonnegative rational estimate down preserves the inequalities because the true distance is an integer. No edit script or alignment has to be returned. When the strings are identical, a successful estimate must be exactly zero.

Truly subquadratic means a fixed positive exponent saving \(\eta\), independent of \(n\). A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log n\), or a stated improvement of the form \(n^{2}/2^{(\log n)^{c}}\) with fixed \(0<c<1\), does not supply such a saving. A polylogarithmic overhead on an already fixed-power saving can be absorbed by decreasing \(\eta\).

The approximation factor is at most three, uniformly over the input size. A guarantee of \(3+\varepsilon\) for every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), or \(3+o(1)\), does not itself establish this endpoint. The main question is existence of some positive runtime saving, not its optimal value.
answer_criterion: Give an algorithm meeting the factor-three guarantee and some fixed positive exponent saving for all inputs in the stated model, or prove that no such randomized algorithm exists. State any hypothesis of a conditional negative result explicitly. An arbitrary constant approximation, a factor exceeding three, an average-case result, or a subpolynomial rather than fixed-power runtime saving is insufficient.
